client: I've been really struggling this past week with this big presentation I have coming up at our annual conference, and honestly, the anxiety has been taking over my whole life. Yesterday during practice I completely blanked — just forgot everything I was supposed to say — and now I can't stop replaying that moment over and over in my head. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to fix anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like this past week has been really draining, and that moment of blanking during practice has lodged itself in your mind in a way that's hard to shake. It makes a lot of sense that you're feeling uncertain about whether talking will help — that skepticism is actually pretty common, and I'm glad you decided to give it a try anyway. I'm curious: when you replay that moment of blanking, what's the thought that tends to come up most strongly for you about what it means?

client: The thought that hits hardest is probably something like, "If I blanked in practice, I'm definitely going to blank in front of everyone at the actual conference, and they're all going to see that I have no idea what I'm talking about." It feels like that one moment is proof of something I've been afraid of for a long time — that I'm just not as competent as people think I am. Like I've been faking it, and this presentation is finally going to expose me.
therapist: What you're describing — this fear of being "found out" — is something many high-achieving people experience, and it even has a name: impostor syndrome. It's worth gently noticing that your mind is treating one difficult practice moment as *proof* of something, when it could also just be evidence that you were stressed and human that day. What would you say to a colleague you respected if *they* came to you having blanked in practice and were convinced it meant they were a fraud?

client: I know what you're getting at, and honestly if a colleague told me that, I'd probably say something like "one bad practice doesn't define you, everyone has off days." But it feels completely different when it's me — like I can extend that understanding to other people no problem, but when I try to apply it to myself it just doesn't stick. I hear the logic, but there's this other voice that immediately comes back with "yeah, but they're actually competent, you're different."
therapist: That gap you're noticing — where compassion flows easily outward but hits a wall when you turn it inward — is such an important and honest observation. That little voice saying "yeah, but you're different" is worth examining, because it's making a pretty big claim: that *everyone else* who doubts themselves is just having an off day, but *your* self-doubt is uniquely accurate and trustworthy. What actual evidence, over time, would you say exists that speaks to your competence — not the feeling of competence, but concrete moments or feedback from others?

client: I mean, there are things — last year my manager specifically told me my quarterly report was the clearest one the team had produced, and a few colleagues have come to me asking for advice on projects because they said they trust my judgment. But when I try to hold onto those moments right now, they feel kind of distant and almost like they don't count, like maybe people were just being polite or I got lucky those times. It's frustrating because I can list the evidence and still not feel any differently about the presentation.
therapist: It's really frustrating to do everything "right" — listing the evidence, recognizing the logic — and still feel stuck, and that frustration makes a lot of sense. What you're describing is actually a core feature of anxiety: it has a way of discounting positive evidence almost automatically, treating praise as luck or politeness while treating one blank moment as absolute truth. It might be worth asking yourself: if you applied the *same* skepticism to the negative evidence — "maybe I blanked because I was overtired, not because I'm incompetent" — what would that change about the story you're telling yourself?

client: I think if I'm being honest, applying that same skepticism to the blanking moment would make the story a little less catastrophic — like maybe it really was just a bad night and not some fundamental truth about me. But I guess my worry is that this kind of reframing feels almost too neat, like I'm just talking myself into feeling better without actually fixing the problem of potentially blanking again at the real conference. What if I do all this mental work and then I actually do freeze up on the day — doesn't that just prove the negative voice was right all along?
therapist: That's a really thoughtful distinction you're making — there's a difference between *feeling* more confident and actually being *prepared*, and it makes sense that you don't want reframing to just be a comfort blanket. But it's worth separating two things: the mental work we're doing isn't about guaranteeing you won't freeze, it's about making sure that *if* you do have a tough moment, the story you tell yourself afterward doesn't spiral into "this proves I'm a fraud." What practical preparation — things like rehearsal strategies or having a recovery plan for if you lose your place — would help you feel like you're addressing the real-world side of this alongside the mental side?

client: I think having a recovery plan actually makes some sense to me — like knowing in advance what I'll do if I lose my place, rather than just hoping it doesn't happen. Maybe something like having a few key notes on a card or just pausing and taking a breath instead of panicking. But I'm a little worried that even if I prepare all of that, the anxiety leading up to the conference is going to be so intense that I won't be able to think straight enough to actually use any of those strategies in the moment.
therapist: It's really encouraging that the recovery plan idea is resonating with you — having that card or that breath as a concrete anchor is exactly the kind of thing that can cut through the noise in a high-pressure moment. The worry about anxiety overwhelming your ability to use these strategies is valid, but here's something worth considering: practicing these recovery moves *while* you're feeling some anxiety — not just when you're calm — actually trains your mind to access them precisely when you need them most. Would you be open to trying a practice run this week where you deliberately let yourself feel the nerves and then practice using one of those anchors, so it starts to feel automatic rather than something you have to remember under pressure?

client: That actually makes a kind of intuitive sense — like the idea that you can't just rehearse in a vacuum and expect it to work when everything feels different. But I'm not sure how I'd deliberately make myself anxious enough to simulate the real thing, because when I practice at home alone it just feels kind of flat and low-stakes no matter what I do. I guess I'm wondering if there's a more realistic way to create that pressure, because I don't want to put in the effort and then find out it wasn't close enough to the real situation to actually help.
therapist: You're thinking about this really practically, and that instinct to want the preparation to actually transfer to the real situation is a smart one. One effective way to raise the stakes is to practice in front of real people — even just one or two colleagues or friends — because the social element tends to activate that same self-conscious anxiety much more than practicing alone does. Would it feel manageable to set up even one small "audience" practice before the conference, and maybe even deliberately fumble at some point during it so you can practice using your recovery anchor in a realistic moment?

client: The idea of practicing in front of people makes sense, but honestly just thinking about asking someone to be my audience already feels embarrassing — like I'm admitting I need extra help, and I worry they'll think less of me before I've even given the presentation. I do have one colleague I trust a bit more than others, so maybe that's where I'd start, but I'm not sure I could bring myself to deliberately fumble on purpose because it feels like it would just reinforce the fear rather than help with it. Can you help me understand a bit more why intentionally messing up is supposed to help rather than just making the anxiety worse?
therapist: The embarrassment around asking for help is so understandable, and it actually connects directly to that impostor fear — as though needing practice is evidence of inadequacy, when really it's just what competent people *do* to prepare well. On the deliberate fumbling: the idea isn't to reinforce failure, but to break the spell that a mistake is catastrophic — when you stumble and then *recover* in front of your trusted colleague, your nervous system gets real evidence that a blank moment isn't the end of the world, which is something no amount of smooth practice can teach. What do you think it would feel like on the other side of that conversation with your colleague — if you asked and they responded with support rather than judgment?

client: If my colleague responded with support, I think I'd probably feel relieved but also a little raw — like I'd exposed something I usually keep hidden and there's no taking it back. I can actually imagine her being kind about it, which is maybe why she's the one I'm even considering asking. But I think the harder part is that even if it goes well, there's still this voice that would say she was just being nice to spare my feelings, and I'm not sure how to stop that from canceling out whatever good came from the experience.
therapist: That "rawness" you're describing is actually something meaningful — it suggests that reaching out to her would be a genuinely vulnerable act, not a small one, and it makes sense that it feels weighty. What's worth noticing is that the voice dismissing her kindness as "just being polite" is the same voice that discounts your manager's feedback and your colleagues' trust — it's a pattern that's working very hard to make sure no positive evidence ever fully lands. What do you think it would take, even just a little, to hold that voice a bit more lightly — to let her support count as *real* data, even if you can't be 100% certain of her motives?

client: I think what you're pointing out about the pattern is hard to argue with — it does seem like that voice has a kind of veto power over anything positive, and I hadn't really seen it that clearly before. But I guess what it would take to hold it more lightly is something I genuinely don't know how to do, because it's not like I can just decide to trust the evidence more and have that actually work. Is that something that gets easier with practice, or is it more like I need to catch the voice in the act each time and consciously push back on it?
therapist: The fact that you can now *see* that veto pattern so clearly is actually more significant than it might feel right now — awareness really is the first step, because you can't challenge something you haven't noticed yet. It's a bit of both things you mentioned: over time it does get more automatic, but in the beginning it really is about catching the voice in the act, naming it ("there's that discounting pattern again"), and consciously asking whether you'd apply the same standard to anyone else. Would it feel useful to start small this week — just noticing once or twice when that voice shows up and writing it down, not to fix it yet, but just to build that muscle of catching it in real time?
